newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE-Bogart's Casablanca transformed into financial hub.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bogart's Casablanca transformed into financial hub.

text.p: They're planning to open Humphrey Bogart's piano bar, Rick's Cafe, in Casablanca to bring back to the Moroccan city the romance of an era of more than 50 years ago.
In fact Bogart and Ingrid Bergman, whose film "Casablanca" enshrined the city in the hearts of romantics everywhere, would have trouble finding the place.
Only the title came from the city, which has changed immeasurably since the film was made in 1942.

"A small part of it was shot in Tangier, in northern Morocco, and the rest in Hollywood...Many foreigners come to us and say they want to see the bar run by Bogart in the film, but the place doesn't exist," said Mohamed Abid Senhaji.
Senhaji, president of a promotional group for the city, said his organisation planned to open a bar with the same name and give certificates to people coming on nostalgic pilgrimages.

Much of the Moroccan ambiance that surrounded the bar in the film did reflect Casablanca at the time. But a lot has vanished from the city, which has been transformed into the country's financial centre -- a loss that Senhaji regrets.
"Very few people are keen to preserve the city's style, which was mostly French. Promoters speculate, they want to get rich rapidly and it is often at the expense of the city," he told Reuters.
Officially, the city with its high-rise buildings, de luxe hotels and 19 cinemas now has some four million people, but Senhaji said: "I think the real figure could go up to six million."
FILM WASN'T MADE IN CASABLANCA

Despite the fact that its most enduring symbol, the movie, was not shot there, Casablanca has its own dates in history. First named Anfa after its port, it became Casablanca in the 15th Century under the Portuguese and the Spanish invaders.
It witnessed the Allied landings in 1942 after the Germans bombed part of the city, the headquarters of American soldiers.
"The Americans and France's General (Charles) De Gaulle teamed up to prevent the Germans from taking Morocco, which was a strategic passage to Europe," said Senhaji.

In 1943 U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt, Britain's Prime Minister Winston Churchill and De Gaulle met in Casablanca to issue the ultimatum for the unconditional surrender of the Axis powers in the middle of World War Two.
Their meeting was officially held at Anfa Hotel, now partly destroyed.

"In fact it was held at a villa nearby, called Essaada (Happiness) because Roosevelt was unable to climb the stairs," Senhaji said, adding: "The American embassy wanted to buy it, but the (Moroccan) owner, knowing what was at stake, overbid the price."
Senhaji said the syndicate intended to build a memorial on the hotel site but was still waiting for official approval.
WIDE GULF BETWEEN RICH AND POOR
Meanwhile, as many look to a vanishing past, Casablanca moves ahead at its own swift pace. The wealthy young drive late-model cars, talk on cellular phones and give big parties.
Some head off to the United States or Canada to study.
But in a constant reminder of wealth disparities, young boys beg at the main railway station and women with babies sit on pavements seeking coins to buy bread.
On the way into the city are the slums, where the Statistics Directorate estimates about 70,000 live.
In the shantytowns lining each side of the railway lines, chequered washing hangs and women work in mud lanes to keep the outside of their homes clean.

But a few entrepreneurial shantytown dwellers might even have a chance to catch Bogart and Bergman recycled on international television networks. On some scattered roofs satellite dishes have sprung up, their sets apparently powered by car batteries.
